title: Source-distance links to butterfly reappearance weakened within species-site pairs in Britain in 1980-2021
abstract: Nearby recorded populations predicted butterfly reappearance across sites. We tested whether changes in that distance predicted reappearance within the same species at the same site. Raw UKBMS indices and public locations gave 16,002 three-zero-year risk windows, 804 sites, 48 taxa and 2,173 repeated-positive outcome windows. A linear probability model with site, species and year effects gave -2.45 percentage points per doubling of one plus source distance in km (95% interval -3.47 to -1.42). With species-site and species-year effects it gave -0.22 (-1.36 to +0.92). The same-sample coefficient difference was +2.22 points (1.42 to 3.03). Three nonoverlapping year phases gave different signs. In a joint model, a source map fully after the outcome had a negative link while past distance had no clear link. These results weaken a direct supply interpretation of the spatial marker. They do not rule out dispersal limits: source-map error can attenuate changes, and local habitat and detection remain unmeasured. No thermal-debt fraction or warming effect is estimated. Code, aggregate evidence, input hashes and external retrieval instructions are included.

display.caption: Source-distance slopes with 95% recipient-block intervals. Pair controls greatly reduce the pooled association. Nonoverlapping year phases differ in sign. These are associations in selected index records.

citations.reason: Tests its unresolved stable species-site confounding using repeated risk windows and pair effects; does not refit its model.
